claims.claim: ACR-12::GFP puncta are distributed throughout the length of the posterior DD5 dendrite in the egl-20(n585) mutant.
claims.source: Indeed, we observed that the ACR-12::GFP puncta are distributed throughout the length of the posterior DD5 dendrite (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The length of the DD5 postsynaptic domain is determined by the length of DD5 posterior dendrite.
claims.source: However, our results suggest that, unlike presynaptic tiling which is largely unaffected by the DD5 axon overextension in the egl-20(n585) mutant, the length of the DD5 postsynaptic domain is determined by the length of DD5 posterior dendrite.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a suggestion based on the results.

claims.claim: Semaphorin-Plexin signaling mediated by PLX-1/Plexin, RAP-2/Rap2A, and MIG-15/TNIK is crucial for the presynaptic tiling of two DA-class cholinergic motor neurons.
claims.source: Previously we showed that Semaphorin-Plexin signaling mediated by PLX-1/Plexin, RAP-2/Rap2A, and MIG-15/TNIK is crucial for the presynaptic tiling of two DA-class cholinergic motor neurons (Chen et al., 2018; Mizumoto and Shen, 2013a).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2018 and Mizumoto and Shen, 2013a.

claims.claim: plx-1(nc36); egl-20(n585) double mutants do not exhibit a presynaptic tiling defect between DD5 and DD6 neurons.
claims.source: However, we did not observe a presynaptic tiling defect between DD5 and DD6 neurons in the double mutants of plx-1(nc36); egl-20(n585), egl-20(n585); rap-2(gk11), and egl-20(n585); mig-15(rh148) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the presynaptic tiling between DD5 and DD6 is controlled by another mechanism.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: egl-20(n585); rap-2(gk11) double mutants do not exhibit a presynaptic tiling defect between DD5 and DD6 neurons.
claims.source: However, we did not observe a presynaptic tiling defect between DD5 and DD6 neurons in the double mutants of plx-1(nc36); egl-20(n585), egl-20(n585); rap-2(gk11), and egl-20(n585); mig-15(rh148) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the presynaptic tiling between DD5 and DD6 is controlled by another mechanism.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: egl-20(n585); mig-15(rh148) double mutants do not exhibit a presynaptic tiling defect between DD5 and DD6 neurons.
claims.source: However, we did not observe a presynaptic tiling defect between DD5 and DD6 neurons in the double mutants of plx-1(nc36); egl-20(n585), egl-20(n585); rap-2(gk11), and egl-20(n585); mig-15(rh148) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the presynaptic tiling between DD5 and DD6 is controlled by another mechanism.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The presynaptic tiling between DD5 and DD6 is controlled by a mechanism different from Semaphorin-Plexin signaling.
claims.source: However, we did not observe a presynaptic tiling defect between DD5 and DD6 neurons in the double mutants of plx-1(nc36); egl-20(n585), egl-20(n585); rap-2(gk11), and egl-20(n585); mig-15(rh148) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the presynaptic tiling between DD5 and DD6 is controlled by another mechanism.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a suggestion based on the lack of presynaptic tiling defects in the mutants.

claims.claim: Gap junctions consisting of INX proteins are formed in the regions of minimal axonal and dendritic overlap between DD neurons according to EM studies.
claims.source: Previous EM studies have shown that gap junctions consisting of INX proteins are formed in the regions of minimal axonal and dendritic overlap between DD neurons where presynaptic and postsynaptic tiling are established (White et al., 1976; White et al., 1986).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to White et al., 1976 and White et al., 1986.

claims.claim: Gap junctions between DD neurons play crucial roles in electrical coupling during sinusoidal locomotion.
claims.source: These gap junctions play crucial roles in electrical coupling between DD neurons during sinusoidal locomotion (Kawano et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kawano et al., 2011.

claims.claim: DD neurons express at least six INX genes: inx-1, inx-2, inx-10, inx-14, unc-7, and unc-9.
claims.source: DD neurons express at least six INX genes, inx-1, inx-2, inx-10, inx-14, unc-7, and unc-9 (Altun et al., 2009; Spencer et al., 2011; Taylor et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Altun et al., 2009, Spencer et al., 2011, and Taylor et al., 2021.

claims.claim: Double mutants of egl-20(n585) and unc-9(e101) exhibit a significant presynaptic tiling defect.
claims.source: Among these six innexins, double mutants of egl-20(n585) and unc-9(e101 or tm5479) null mutants exhibited a significant presynaptic tiling defect (Figure 2B and E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B and E.

claims.claim: Double mutants of egl-20(n585) and unc-9(tm5479) exhibit a significant presynaptic tiling defect.
claims.source: Among these six innexins, double mutants of egl-20(n585) and unc-9(e101 or tm5479) null mutants exhibited a significant presynaptic tiling defect (Figure 2B and E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B and E.

claims.claim: Ectopic DD5 presynaptic puncta are formed in the DD5 posterior axon that overextended into the DD6 axonal region in egl-20(n585); unc-9(e101) mutants.
claims.source: Ectopic DD5 presynaptic puncta are formed in the DD5 posterior axon that overextended into the DD6 axonal region, which creates intermingled patterning of DD5 and DD6 presynaptic puncta (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Ectopic DD5 presynaptic puncta in egl-20(n585); unc-9(e101) mutants create intermingled patterning of DD5 and DD6 presynaptic puncta.
claims.source: Ectopic DD5 presynaptic puncta are formed in the DD5 posterior axon that overextended into the DD6 axonal region, which creates intermingled patterning of DD5 and DD6 presynaptic puncta (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The presynaptic tiling defect in egl-20(n585); unc-9(e101) mutants is fully rescued by the Pegl-20::egl-20 transgene.
claims.source: The presynaptic tiling defect in the egl-20(n585); unc-9(e101) mutants is fully rescued by the Pegl-20::egl-20 transgene, which rescues the axonal tiling defect (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), suggesting that overextension of DD5 posterior axon is necessary for observing the effect of unc-9 in presynaptic patterning (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by rescue data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Overextension of DD5 posterior axon is necessary for observing the effect of unc-9 in presynaptic patterning.
claims.source: The presynaptic tiling defect in the egl-20(n585); unc-9(e101) mutants is fully rescued by the Pegl-20::egl-20 transgene, which rescues the axonal tiling defect (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), suggesting that overextension of DD5 posterior axon is necessary for observing the effect of unc-9 in presynaptic patterning (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a suggestion based on the rescue experiment.

claims.claim: unc-9(e101) single mutants do not exhibit a presynaptic tiling defect.
claims.source: Consistently, unc-9(e101) single mutants did not exhibit presynaptic tiling defect due to the normal axonal tiling in the presence of egl-20 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Loss of unc-9 does not enhance the axonal tiling defect of egl-20(n585) mutants.
claims.source: Importantly, loss of unc-9 does not enhance the axonal tiling defect of egl-20(n585) mutants (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The presynaptic tiling defect in egl-20(n585); unc-9(e101) double mutants is not due to an increased axonal tiling defect.
claims.source: Therefore, the presynaptic tiling defect in the egl-20(n585); unc-9(e101) double mutants is not due to an increased axonal tiling defect.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion based on the observation that loss of unc-9 does not enhance axonal tiling defect.

claims.claim: The overgrowth of the DD5 posterior axon in egl-20(n585) mutant is present at the second larval (L2) stage.
claims.source: DD neurons undergo remodeling at the end of the first larval (L1) stage, when the dorsal neurites switch their fate from dendrite to axon (White et al., 1978). We found that the overgrowth of the DD5 posterior axon in egl-20(n585) mutant is present at the second larval (L2) stage (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: A significant presynaptic tiling defect is observed at the L2 stage in egl-20(n585); unc-9(e101) mutant.
claims.source: We observed a significant presynaptic tiling defect at the L2 stage in egl-20(n585); unc-9(e101) mutant (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: unc-9 is required for the establishment of presynaptic tiling.
claims.source: As the remodeling completes by the end of L2 stage, this result suggests that unc-9 is required for the establishment of presynaptic tiling.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a suggestion based on the observation of presynaptic tiling defect at L2 stage.

claims.claim: Heat-shock-induced expression of unc-9 at the L2 stage after presynaptic tiling is established does not rescue the presynaptic tiling defects in egl-20(n585); unc-9(e101).
claims.source: To determine if unc-9 is also required for the maintenance of presynaptic tiling, we conducted rescue experiments using a heat shock promoter. We found that the heat-shock-induced expression of unc-9 at the L2 stage after presynaptic tiling is established did not rescue the presynaptic tiling defects in egl-20(n585); unc-9(e101).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by rescue experiment data.

claims.claim: unc-9 is required for the establishment but not maintenance of presynaptic tiling of DD5 and DD6.
claims.source: This result is consistent with the idea that unc-9 is required for the establishment of the presynaptic tiling of DD5 and DD6 (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as consistent with the heat shock rescue experiment results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: UNC-9::7×GFP is localized at the anterior tip of the DD6 axon in wild type animals.
claims.source: In wild type animals, UNC-9::7×GFP is localized at the anterior tip of the DD6 axon and dendrite (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 2F.

claims.claim: UNC-9::7×GFP is localized at the anterior tip of the DD6 dendrite in wild type animals.
claims.source: In wild type animals, UNC-9::7×GFP is localized at the anterior tip of the DD6 axon and dendrite (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 2F.

claims.claim: UNC-9::7×GFP localization at the anterior tip of the DD6 axon and dendrite is observed in L1 animals.
claims.source: Consistent with the requirement of unc-9 in the establishment of presynaptic tiling, UNC-9::7×GFP localization at the anterior tip of the DD6 axon and dendrite is observed in L1 animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claims.claim: In the egl-20(n585) mutant, UNC-9::7×GFP is localized at the anterior tip of DD6 axon and dendrite similar to wild type.
claims.source: In the egl-20(n585) mutant, in which DD5 axon overextends to the DD6 axonal region, UNC-9::7×GFP was localized at the anterior tip of DD6 axon and dendrite similar to wild type, even though the signal intensity of the UNC-9::7×GFP at the tip of DD6 axon was slightly reduced (Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claims.claim: The signal intensity of UNC-9::7×GFP at the tip of DD6 axon is slightly reduced in the egl-20(n585) mutant.
claims.source: In the egl-20(n585) mutant, in which DD5 axon overextends to the DD6 axonal region, UNC-9::7×GFP was localized at the anterior tip of DD6 axon and dendrite similar to wild type, even though the signal intensity of the UNC-9::7×GFP at the tip of DD6 axon was slightly reduced (Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claims.claim: The slight reduction of UNC-9 localization at the presynaptic tiling border may account for the subtle presynaptic tiling defect of the egl-20(n585) single mutant.
claims.source: The slight reduction of UNC-9 localization at the presynaptic tiling border may account for the subtle presynaptic tiling defect of the egl-20(n585) single mutant (Figure 1H).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a possible explanation for the subtle presynaptic tiling defect.

claims.claim: Overextension of DD5 axon and dendrite in the egl-20 mutant does not affect the overall position of UNC-9 gap junctions formed between DD5 and DD6 axons and dendrites.
claims.source: This result suggests that overextension of DD5 axon and dendrite in the egl-20 mutant does not affect the overall position of UNC-9 gap junctions formed between DD5 and DD6 axons and dendrites.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a suggestion based on the observation of UNC-9 localization in egl-20 mutant.

claims.claim: UNC-9 functions as a positional cue to define the presynaptic tiling border between DD5 and DD6 in egl-20 mutant background.
claims.source: As presynaptic tiling was largely unaffected in egl-20(n585) single mutant, the UNC-9 localization at the presynaptic tiling border in egl-20(n585) mutant suggests that UNC-9 functions as a positional cue to define the presynaptic tiling border between DD5 and DD6 in egl-20 mutant background.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a suggestion based on the observation of UNC-9 localization and presynaptic tiling pattern.

claims.claim: The DD5 posterior postsynaptic domain is significantly longer in the egl-20(n585) single mutant.
claims.source: While the UNC-9::7×GFP localization appears to be unaffected in the dendrite, the DD5 posterior postsynaptic domain, judged by ACR-12::GFP, is significantly longer in the egl-20(n585) single mutant (Figure 2G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), suggesting that unc-9 does not control postsynaptic patterning of DD5.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 2G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: unc-9 does not control postsynaptic patterning of DD5.
claims.source: While the UNC-9::7×GFP localization appears to be unaffected in the dendrite, the DD5 posterior postsynaptic domain, judged by ACR-12::GFP, is significantly longer in the egl-20(n585) single mutant (Figure 2G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), suggesting that unc-9 does not control postsynaptic patterning of DD5.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a suggestion based on the observation that postsynaptic domain is longer despite normal UNC-9 localization.

claims.claim: GFP::UNC-9 expressed under the DD-neuron-specific promoter flp-13 is localized to the anterior tip of the DD6 axon and dendrite.
claims.source: We found that GFP::UNC-9 expressed under the DD-neuron-specific promoter, flp-13, was localized to the anterior tip of the DD6 axon and dendrite, similar to UNC-9::7×GFP (Figure 2H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 2H.

claims.claim: UNC-9::7×GFP puncta are distributed throughout the DA9 axon.
claims.source: We therefore examined the localization of UNC-9::7×GFP in the DA9 neuron by expressing GFP1-10 under the DA9-neuron-specific promoter, itr-1. Unlike in DD neurons where UNC-9::7×GFP is almost exclusively detected at axonal and dendritic tiling borders between neighboring DD neurons, UNC-9::7×GFP puncta was distributed throughout the DA9 axon (Figure 2—figure supplement 7).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 7.

claims.claim: UNC-9::7×GFP puncta are often associated with the presynaptic varicosity in DA9 neurons.
claims.source: The UNC-9::7×GFP puncta are often associated with the presynaptic varicosity which is reminiscent to the perisynaptic localization of endogenous UNC-9 in DD neurons (Yeh et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as an observation with citation to Yeh et al., 2009.

claims.claim: UNC-9::7×GFP is consistently localized at the distal end of DA9 dendrites.
claims.source: In addition, UNC-9::7×GFP was consistently localized at the distal end of DA9 dendrites.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as an observation.

claims.claim: unc-9(e101) mutant does not exhibit a presynaptic tiling defect between DA8 and DA9.
claims.source: We also found that unc-9(e101) mutant did not exhibit a presynaptic tiling defect between DA8 and DA9 (Figure 2—figure supplement 7).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 7.

claims.claim: Each motor neuron class uses distinct mechanisms for controlling the presynaptic tiling pattern.
claims.source: While we do not exclude the possibility that other innexins control presynaptic tiling of DA8 and DA9 neurons, our result suggests that each motor neuron class uses distinct mechanisms for controlling the presynaptic tiling pattern.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a suggestion based on the observation that unc-9 does not affect DA8/DA9 presynaptic tiling.

claims.claim: Gap junction clustering is controlled by neurexin-like receptor 1 (NLR-1) and tight junction associated protein ZO-1 in C. elegans and zebrafish.
claims.source: Recent work in C. elegans and zebrafish showed that gap junction clustering is controlled by a neurexin-like receptor 1 (NLR-1) and a tight junction associated protein ZO-1 (Meng and Yan, 2020; Lasseigne et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Meng and Yan, 2020 and Lasseigne et al., 2021.

claims.claim: Clustered UNC-9 localization depends on NLR-1 in the nerve ring of C. elegans.
claims.source: In the nerve ring of C. elegans, clustered UNC-9 localization depends on NLR-1 (Meng and Yan, 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Meng and Yan, 2020.

claims.claim: Cx35.5 and Cx34.1 localization at the club ending synapses depend on ZO1b in zebrafish.
claims.source: In zebrafish, Cx35.5 and Cx34.1 localization at the club ending synapses depend on ZO1b (Lasseigne et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lasseigne et al., 2021.

claims.claim: nlr-1 and zoo-1 are expressed in DD neurons.
claims.source: While both nlr-1 and zoo-1, an ortholog of ZO-1, are expressed in DD neurons (Taylor et al., 2021), the localization of UNC-9::7×GFP at the anterior tip of the DD6 axon was unaffected in the nlr-1(gk366849) and zoo-1(tm4133) null mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 6), suggesting that UNC-9 localization at the axonal tiling border is independent of the known regulators of gap junction clustering.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Taylor et al., 2021.

claims.claim: The localization of UNC-9::7×GFP at the anterior tip of the DD6 axon is unaffected in nlr-1(gk366849) null mutants.
claims.source: While both nlr-1 and zoo-1, an ortholog of ZO-1, are expressed in DD neurons (Taylor et al., 2021), the localization of UNC-9::7×GFP at the anterior tip of the DD6 axon was unaffected in the nlr-1(gk366849) and zoo-1(tm4133) null mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 6), suggesting that UNC-9 localization at the axonal tiling border is independent of the known regulators of gap junction clustering.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claims.claim: The localization of UNC-9::7×GFP at the anterior tip of the DD6 axon is unaffected in zoo-1(tm4133) null mutants.
claims.source: While both nlr-1 and zoo-1, an ortholog of ZO-1, are expressed in DD neurons (Taylor et al., 2021), the localization of UNC-9::7×GFP at the anterior tip of the DD6 axon was unaffected in the nlr-1(gk366849) and zoo-1(tm4133) null mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 6), suggesting that UNC-9 localization at the axonal tiling border is independent of the known regulators of gap junction clustering.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claims.claim: UNC-9 localization at the axonal tiling border is independent of the known regulators of gap junction clustering.
claims.source: While both nlr-1 and zoo-1, an ortholog of ZO-1, are expressed in DD neurons (Taylor et al., 2021), the localization of UNC-9::7×GFP at the anterior tip of the DD6 axon was unaffected in the nlr-1(gk366849) and zoo-1(tm4133) null mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 6), suggesting that UNC-9 localization at the axonal tiling border is independent of the known regulators of gap junction clustering.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a suggestion based on the observation that UNC-9 localization is unaffected in nlr-1 and zoo-1 mutants.

claims.claim: UNC-9::7×GFP puncta at the DD6 dendrite have a tendency to localize slightly posteriorly from the tip of the DD6 dendrite in zoo-1(tm4133) mutant.
claims.source: We note that UNC-9::7×GFP puncta at the DD6 dendrite had a tendency to localize slightly posteriorly from the tip of the DD6 dendrite in zoo-1(tm4133) mutant (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claims.claim: egl-20(n585); nlr-1(gk366849) mutants do not exhibit a presynaptic tiling defect.
claims.source: Consistent with the unaffected UNC-9 localization, we did not observe a presynaptic tiling defect in the egl-20(n585); nlr-1(gk366849) and egl-20(n585); zoo-1(tm4133) mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: egl-20(n585); zoo-1(tm4133) mutants do not exhibit a presynaptic tiling defect.
claims.source: Consistent with the unaffected UNC-9 localization, we did not observe a presynaptic tiling defect in the egl-20(n585); nlr-1(gk366849) and egl-20(n585); zoo-1(tm4133) mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: There is a slight reduction in UNC-9::7×GFP signal intensity in unc-104(e1265) mutant without affecting the overall localization pattern at the anterior tip of DD6 axon.
claims.source: We also examined UNC-9::7×GFP localization in the mutant of neuronal kinesin/KIF1A, unc-104(e1265), in which axonal transport is severely compromised (Hall and Hedgecock, 1991). We found a slight reduction in UNC-9::7×GFP signal intensity without affecting the overall localization pattern at the anterior tip of DD6 axon (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claims.claim: UNC-9 localization at the axonal tiling border is mediated by an unknown mechanism.
claims.source: These results suggest that UNC-9 localization at the axonal tiling border is mediated by an unknown mechanism, and its transport may partially depend on UNC-104/KIF1A.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a suggestion based on the observations in various mutants.

claims.claim: UNC-9 transport may partially depend on UNC-104/KIF1A.
claims.source: These results suggest that UNC-9 localization at the axonal tiling border is mediated by an unknown mechanism, and its transport may partially depend on UNC-104/KIF1A.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a suggestion based on the slight reduction of UNC-9 signal in unc-104 mutant.

claims.claim: unc-9 is expressed broadly in the nervous system and non-neuronal tissues, including DD neurons and their postsynaptic body wall muscles.
claims.source: unc-9 is expressed broadly in the nervous system and non-neuronal tissues, including the DD neurons and their postsynaptic body wall muscles (Yeh et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yeh et al., 2009.

claims.claim: Pan-neuronal expression of unc-9 under the rgef-1 promoter rescues the presynaptic tiling defect of egl-20(n585); unc-9(e101) double mutants.
claims.source: Pan-neuronal expression of unc-9 under the rgef-1 promoter rescued the presynaptic tiling defect of the egl-20(n585); unc-9(e101) double mutants (Figure 3A and C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by rescue data shown in Figure 3A and C.

claims.claim: unc-9 expression in the presynaptic DD neurons using the flp-13 promoter rescues the presynaptic tiling defect of egl-20(n585); unc-9(e101) double mutants.
claims.source: Similarly, unc-9 expression in the presynaptic DD neurons using the flp-13 promoter but not in the postsynaptic body wall muscles using the myo-3 promoter rescued the presynaptic tiling defect (Figure 3B and C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by rescue data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claims.claim: unc-9 expression in the postsynaptic body wall muscles using the myo-3 promoter does not rescue the presynaptic tiling defect of egl-20(n585); unc-9(e101) double mutants.
claims.source: Similarly, unc-9 expression in the presynaptic DD neurons using the flp-13 promoter but not in the postsynaptic body wall muscles using the myo-3 promoter rescued the presynaptic tiling defect (Figure 3B and C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by rescue data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claims.claim: unc-9 controls tiled presynaptic patterning in the presynaptic DD neurons.
claims.source: These results suggest that unc-9 controls tiled presynaptic patterning in the presynaptic DD neurons.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a suggestion based on the tissue-specific rescue experiments.

claims.claim: Expression of unc-9 specifically in the DD6 neuron using the plx-2 promoter does not rescue the presynaptic tiling defect between DD5 and DD6.
claims.source: Expression of unc-9 specifically in the DD6 neuron using the plx-2 promoter did not rescue the presynaptic tiling defect between DD5 and DD6 (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by rescue data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: unc-9 is required in both DD5 and DD6 neurons to control tiled presynaptic patterning between DD5 and DD6.
claims.source: These results suggest that unc-9 is required in both DD5 and DD6 neurons to control tiled presynaptic patterning between DD5 and DD6.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a suggestion based on the observation that DD6-specific expression does not rescue the defect.

claims.claim: UNC-1/stomatin is essential for opening the UNC-9 gap junction channels.
claims.source: It has been shown that UNC-1/stomatin is essential for opening the UNC-9 gap junction channels (Chen et al., 2007; Jang et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2007 and Jang et al., 2017.

claims.claim: In unc-1 loss-of-function mutants, UNC-9 gap junction channel activity is completely abolished.
claims.source: In the loss-of-function mutants of unc-1, UNC-9 gap junction channel activity is completely abolished (Chen et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2007.

claims.claim: unc-1 mutants exhibit a kinky locomotion (kinker) phenotype similar to unc-9 mutants.
claims.source: Due to the defective UNC-9 gap junction channel activity, unc-1 mutants exhibit a kinky locomotion (kinker) phenotype similar to unc-9 mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: egl-20(n585); unc-1(e719) double mutants do not exhibit a presynaptic tiling defect.
claims.source: Interestingly, unlike egl-20(n585); unc-9(e101) double mutants, egl-20(n585); unc-1(e719) double mutants did not exhibit a presynaptic tiling defect (Figure 4A and D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A and D.

claims.claim: egl-20(n585) unc-24(miz225) double mutants do not exhibit a presynaptic tiling defect.
claims.source: Similar to egl-20(n585); unc-1(e719) mutants, egl-20(n585) unc-24(miz225) double mutants and egl-20(n585) unc-24(miz226); unc-1(e719) triple mutants did not exhibit a presynaptic tiling defect (Figure 4B, C and D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B, C, and D.

claims.claim: egl-20(n585) unc-24(miz226); unc-1(e719) triple mutants do not exhibit a presynaptic tiling defect.
claims.source: Similar to egl-20(n585); unc-1(e719) mutants, egl-20(n585) unc-24(miz225) double mutants and egl-20(n585) unc-24(miz226); unc-1(e719) triple mutants did not exhibit a presynaptic tiling defect (Figure 4B, C and D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B, C, and D.

claims.claim: UNC-9's function in controlling presynaptic tiling between DD5 and DD6 is independent of its gap junction channel activity.
claims.source: These results raise the possibility that UNC-9's function in controlling presynaptic tiling between DD5 and DD6 is independent of its gap junction channel activity.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a possibility based on the observation that unc-1 mutants do not exhibit presynaptic tiling defects.

claims.claim: A mutant INX-6 carrying an 18-amino-acid deletion in its amino-terminal intracellular domain forms constitutively closed gap junction channels according to cryo-EM studies.
claims.source: Previous cryo-EM studies using C. elegans INX-6/INX have shown that a mutant INX-6 carrying an 18-amino-acid deletion in its amino-terminal intracellular domain forms constitutively closed gap junction channels (Burendei et al., 2020; Oshima et al., 2016a; Oshima et al., 2016b).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Burendei et al., 2020, Oshima et al., 2016a, and Oshima et al., 2016b.

claims.claim: UNC-9(ΔN18)::GFP expressed in DD neurons is localized at the anterior tip of DD6 axon.
claims.source: Similar to wild type UNC-9::GFP, UNC-9(ΔN18)::GFP expressed in the DD neurons was localized at the anterior tip of DD6 axon, the putative gap junction site between DD5 and DD6 (Figure 5A and B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 5A and B.

claims.claim: The 18 amino acid deletion in UNC-9(ΔN18) does not alter the synthesis or subcellular localization of the protein.
claims.source: This result indicates that the 18 amino acid deletion does not alter either the synthesis or subcellular localization of the UNC-9(ΔN18) protein.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as an indication based on the observation of normal localization of UNC-9(ΔN18)::GFP.

claims.claim: Pan-neuronal expression of unc-9(ΔN18) rescues the presynaptic tiling defect of egl-20(n585); unc-9(e101) mutants.
claims.source: Surprisingly, both pan-neuronal and DD neuron-specific expression of unc-9(Δ18N) rescued the presynaptic tiling defect of egl-20(n585); unc-9(e101) mutants (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by rescue data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: DD neuron-specific expression of unc-9(ΔN18) rescues the presynaptic tiling defect of egl-20(n585); unc-9(e101) mutants.
claims.source: Surprisingly, both pan-neuronal and DD neuron-specific expression of unc-9(Δ18N) rescued the presynaptic tiling defect of egl-20(n585); unc-9(e101) mutants (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by rescue data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Pan-neuronal expression of wild type unc-9 rescues the kinker phenotype of unc-9(e101) mutant.
claims.source: Importantly, pan-neuronal expression of wild type unc-9 but not unc-9(ΔN18) rescued the kinker phenotype of the unc-9(e101) mutant (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Pan-neuronal expression of unc-9(ΔN18) does not rescue the kinker phenotype of unc-9(e101) mutant.
claims.source: Importantly, pan-neuronal expression of wild type unc-9 but not unc-9(ΔN18) rescued the kinker phenotype of the unc-9(e101) mutant (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The failure to rescue the locomotion defects of unc-9 mutants by unc-9(ΔN18) strongly suggests that UNC-9(ΔN18) forms a defective, likely a constitutively closed, gap junction channel.
claims.source: As the locomotion defects of unc-9 mutants are largely due to the defective gap junction channel activity (Kawano et al., 2011), the failure to rescue the locomotion defects of unc-9 mutants by unc-9(Δ18N) strongly suggests that UNC-9(ΔN18) forms a defective, likely a constitutively closed, gap junction channel.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a strong suggestion based on the failure to rescue locomotion defects and citation to Kawano et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Wild type UNC-9 restores junctional current in unc-9(e101) mutants.
claims.source: As expected, wild type UNC-9 restored the junctional current in the unc-9(e101) mutants, while unc-9(e101) mutants expressing unc-9(ΔN18) completely lacked the intra-quadrant coupling similar to unc-9(e101) mutants (Figure 5F–H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5F-H.

claims.claim: unc-9(e101) mutants expressing unc-9(ΔN18) completely lack intra-quadrant coupling similar to unc-9(e101) mutants.
claims.source: As expected, wild type UNC-9 restored the junctional current in the unc-9(e101) mutants, while unc-9(e101) mutants expressing unc-9(ΔN18) completely lacked the intra-quadrant coupling similar to unc-9(e101) mutants (Figure 5F–H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5F-H.

claims.claim: UNC-9(ΔN18) is unable to form functional gap junction channels while maintaining the ability to control tiled presynaptic patterning between DD5 and DD6.
claims.source: These results confirm that UNC-9(ΔN18) is unable to form functional gap junction channels, while maintaining the ability to control tiled presynaptic patterning between DD5 and DD6.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a confirmation based on the electrophysiology and rescue experiments.

claims.claim: unc-9(syb3236 [unc-9(ΔN18)]) mutant animals exhibit a kinker phenotype.
claims.source: Similar to unc-9(e101) mutant, unc-9(syb3236 [unc-9(ΔN18)]) mutant animals exhibit a kinker phenotype (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting that UNC-9(ΔN18) does not form functional gap junction channels.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: unc-9(syb3236 [unc-9(ΔN18)]) mutant does not exhibit a presynaptic tiling defect between DD5 and DD6 in the egl-20(n585) mutant background.
claims.source: Despite the kinker phenotype, unc-9(syb3236 [unc-9(ΔN18)]) mutant did not exhibit a presynaptic tiling defect between DD5 and DD6 in the egl-20(n585) mutant background (Figure 5C and D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5C and D.

claims.claim: The unc-9(ΔN18) deletion does not cause a presynaptic tiling defect in the egl-20(n585); unc-1(miz297) null mutant background where UNC-9 gap junction channel activity is absent.
claims.source: The unc-9(ΔN18) deletion did not cause a presynaptic tiling defect in the egl-20(n585); unc-1(miz297) null mutant background where the UNC-9 gap junction channel activity is absent (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: UNC-9 does not require its gap junction channel activity to control presynaptic tiling.
claims.source: This further confirmed that UNC-9 does not require its gap junction channel activity to control presynaptic tiling.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a confirmation based on the observation that unc-9(ΔN18) does not cause presynaptic tiling defect in unc-1 mutant background.

claims.claim: UNC-9::GFP fusion protein may form constitutively open gap junction channels in muscles.
claims.source: Previously, we showed that an UNC-9::GFP fusion protein may form constitutively open gap junction channels in muscles and that such gap junctions do not require UNC-1 to function (Chen et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2007.

claims.claim: UNC-9::GFP gap junctions do not require UNC-1 to function.
claims.source: Previously, we showed that an UNC-9::GFP fusion protein may form constitutively open gap junction channels in muscles and that such gap junctions do not require UNC-1 to function (Chen et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2007.

claims.claim: The dispensability of UNC-1 to UNC-9::GFP gap junctions has been shown with C. elegans neurons.
claims.source: The dispensability of UNC-1 to UNC-9::GFP gap junctions has also been shown with C. elegans neurons (Jang et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jang et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Muscle expression of unc-9::mTagBFP2 in unc-9(e101) mutant results in a much larger junctional current and conductance than those obtained with wild type unc-9.
claims.source: The muscle expression of unc-9::mTagBFP2 in unc-9(e101) mutant resulted in a much larger Ij and Gj than those obtained with wild type unc-9 (Figure 5F–H), which is reminiscent of our previous observation with unc-9::GFP (Chen et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5F-H and citation to Chen et al., 2007.

claims.claim: Pan-neuronal expression of unc-9::mTagBFP2 rescues the presynaptic patterning defect of egl-20(n585); unc-9(e101) mutant.
claims.source: Similar to unc-9(ΔN18), pan-neuronal expression of unc-9::mTagBFP2 rescued the presynaptic patterning defect of egl-20(n585); unc-9(e101) mutant (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by rescue data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Pan-neuronal expression of unc-9::mTagBFP2 does not rescue the kinker phenotype of unc-9(e101) mutant.
claims.source: Importantly, pan-neuronal expression of unc-9::mTagBFP2 did not rescue the kinker phenotype of unc-9(e101) mutant (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), which is probably because hyperactive gap junction channel activity formed by UNC-9::mTagBFP2 impaired rather than restored the function of the locomotor neural circuit.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Hyperactive gap junction channel activity formed by UNC-9::mTagBFP2 impairs rather than restores the function of the locomotor neural circuit.
claims.source: Importantly, pan-neuronal expression of unc-9::mTagBFP2 did not rescue the kinker phenotype of unc-9(e101) mutant (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), which is probably because hyperactive gap junction channel activity formed by UNC-9::mTagBFP2 impaired rather than restored the function of the locomotor neural circuit.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a probable explanation for the failure to rescue the kinker phenotype.

claims.claim: unc-9(miz81 [unc-9::7×gfp11]) mutants exhibit a kinker phenotype.
claims.source: While UNC-9::7×GFP localizes to the putative gap junction sites between DD5 and DD6 axons, unc-9(miz81 [unc-9::7×gfp11]) mutants exhibit a kinker phenotype (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting that they form defective, likely an open form of gap junctions.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: unc-9(miz81 [unc-9::7×gfp11]) mutants form defective, likely an open form of gap junctions.
claims.source: While UNC-9::7×GFP localizes to the putative gap junction sites between DD5 and DD6 axons, unc-9(miz81 [unc-9::7×gfp11]) mutants exhibit a kinker phenotype (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting that they form defective, likely an open form of gap junctions.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a suggestion based on the kinker phenotype.

claims.claim: egl-20(n585); unc-9(miz81 [unc-9::7×gfp11]) mutant does not exhibit a presynaptic tiling defect.
claims.source: Despite the kinker phenotype, egl-20(n585); unc-9(miz81 [unc-9::7×gfp11]) mutant does not exhibit the presynaptic tiling defect (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: An increased activity of UNC-9 gap junctions does not compromise the physiological role of UNC-9 in controlling the presynaptic tiling pattern.
claims.source: These results suggest that an increased activity of UNC-9 gap junctions does not compromise the physiological role of UNC-9 in controlling the presynaptic tiling pattern.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a suggestion based on the observation that unc-9::mTagBFP2 and unc-9::7×gfp11 can rescue presynaptic tiling defects.

claims.claim: UNC-9 controls presynaptic tiling through a gap junction channel-independent function.
claims.source: Taken together, our results indicate that UNC-9 controls presynaptic tiling through a gap junction channel-independent function.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as an indication based on the collective results from mutant and rescue experiments.

claims.claim: EGL-20/Wnt negatively regulates the length of the posterior axon and dendrite of DD5.
claims.source: We found that EGL-20/Wnt negatively regulates the length of the posterior axon and dendrite of DD5.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a finding in the Discussion section.

claims.claim: Presynaptic tiling requires UNC-9/INX.
claims.source: We showed that presynaptic tiling requires UNC-9/INX, while the position of postsynaptic spines appears to depend on the length of the posterior dendrite.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a finding in the Discussion section.

claims.claim: The position of postsynaptic spines appears to depend on the length of the posterior dendrite.
claims.source: We showed that presynaptic tiling requires UNC-9/INX, while the position of postsynaptic spines appears to depend on the length of the posterior dendrite.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a finding in the Discussion section.

claims.claim: UNC-9 is localized at the presynaptic tiling border between DD5 and DD6 where it forms gap junction channels.
claims.source: UNC-9 is localized at the presynaptic tiling border between DD5 and DD6 where it forms gap junction channels.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a finding in the Discussion section.

claims.claim: The gap junction channel activity of UNC-9 is dispensable for its function in establishing presynaptic tiling.
claims.source: Strikingly, the gap junction channel activity of UNC-9 is dispensable for its function in establishing presynaptic tiling.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a striking finding in the Discussion section.

claims.claim: The presynaptic tiling of DD neurons is governed by two redundant pathways: Wnt-dependent axonal tiling and INX-dependent presynaptic tiling.
claims.source: Therefore, the presynaptic tiling of the DD neurons is governed by two redundant pathways: Wnt-dependent axonal tiling and INX-dependent presynaptic tiling.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion section.

claims.claim: The axonal tiling is dispensable for the presynaptic tiling in DD neurons.
claims.source: However, our observation revealed that the axonal tiling is dispensable for the presynaptic tiling, which is controlled by UNC-9.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as an observation in the Discussion section.

claims.claim: DD neurons are the only GABAergic-class of motor neurons in the dorsal nerve cord.
claims.source: This may be because the DD neurons are the only GABAergic-class of motor neurons in the dorsal nerve cord and thus require more robust control of their synaptic patterning.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a possible explanation for redundant mechanisms.

claims.claim: The redundant mechanisms to tile synapses in DD neurons by Wnt and INX may ensure the proper functions of the DD neurons.
claims.source: As the synapse is the functional unit for this functionality of the DD neurons, the redundant mechanisms to tile synapses in DD neurons by Wnt and INX may ensure the proper functions of the DD neurons.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a possible explanation in the Discussion section.

claims.claim: The degree of presynaptic tiling defect of egl-20(n585); unc-9(e101) mutant is smaller than the degree of axonal tiling defect.
claims.source: The degree of presynaptic tiling defect of egl-20(n585); unc-9(e101) mutant is smaller than the degree of axonal tiling defect, suggesting the presence of additional factors that regulate presynaptic patterning between DD5 and DD6 along with unc-9.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as an observation in the Discussion section.

claims.claim: There are additional factors that regulate presynaptic patterning between DD5 and DD6 along with unc-9.
claims.source: The degree of presynaptic tiling defect of egl-20(n585); unc-9(e101) mutant is smaller than the degree of axonal tiling defect, suggesting the presence of additional factors that regulate presynaptic patterning between DD5 and DD6 along with unc-9.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a suggestion based on the observation of smaller presynaptic tiling defect.

claims.claim: Spatial expression pattern of two Wnt proteins (LIN-44 and EGL-20) defines topographic presynaptic patterning of DA8 and DA9 in the absence of Plexin-dependent presynaptic tiling mechanism.
claims.source: Previously, we showed that spatial expression pattern of two Wnt proteins (LIN-44 and EGL-20) defines topographic presynaptic patterning of DA8 and DA9 in the absence of Plexin-dependent presynaptic tiling mechanism (Mizumoto and Shen, 2013b).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mizumoto and Shen, 2013b.

claims.claim: LIN-44/Wnt may contribute toward the positioning of DD5 synapses in the egl-20; unc-9 mutant.
claims.source: It is therefore possible that LIN-44/Wnt contributes toward the positioning of DD5 synapses in the egl-20; unc-9 mutant.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a possibility in the Discussion section.

claims.claim: The specific subcellular localization of UNC-9 gap junctions at the presynaptic tiling border suggests that UNC-9 acts as a positional cue by forming a highly localized gap junction plaque that locally restricts synapse formation.
claims.source: The specific subcellular localization of UNC-9 gap junctions at the presynaptic tiling border suggests that UNC-9 acts as a positional cue by forming a highly localized gap junction plaque that locally restricts synapse formation.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a suggestion based on the localization pattern of UNC-9.

claims.claim: Loss of unc-9 results in ectopic synapse formation in the distal posterior axonal region of DD5.
claims.source: Indeed, loss of unc-9 results in the ectopic synapse formation in the distal posterior axonal region of DD5.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a confirmation of the hypothesis that UNC-9 restricts synapse formation.

claims.claim: PANX1 inhibits synapse formation in mouse cortical neurons.
claims.source: Consistent with our observations, recent work in mouse cortical neurons showed that PANX1 inhibits synapse formation (Sanchez-Arias et al., 2020; Sanchez-Arias et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sanchez-Arias et al., 2020 and Sanchez-Arias et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Gap junction proteins may have conserved functions as negative regulators for synapse formation.
claims.source: It is therefore possible that gap junction proteins have conserved functions as negative regulators for synapse formation.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a possibility based on observations in C. elegans and mouse.

claims.claim: UNC-9 was shown to localize at the nonjunctional perisynaptic region in DD neurons to regulate active zone differentiation, possibly as hemichannels.
claims.source: Previously, UNC-9 was shown to localize at the nonjunctional perisynaptic region in the DD neurons to regulate active zone differentiation, possibly as hemichannels (Yeh et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yeh et al., 2009.

claims.claim: unc-9's function in promoting presynaptic assembly contrasts with findings that unc-9 restricts synapse formation.
claims.source: unc-9's function in promoting presynaptic assembly contrasts with our findings that unc-9 restricts synapse formation.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a contrast between previous findings and current findings.

claims.claim: Distinct localization of UNC-9 may inhibit or promote synapse formation through distinct downstream molecular pathways.
claims.source: It is possible that distinct localization of UNC-9 may inhibit or promote synapse formation through distinct downstream molecular pathways.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a possibility to reconcile contrasting observations.

claims.claim: Proper actin cytoskeleton formation is essential for synapse formation.
claims.source: While we do not know how UNC-9 locally restricts synapse formation, it is possible that it acts through actin cytoskeleton and its regulators, as proper actin cytoskeleton formation is essential for synapse formation (Aiken and Holzbaur, 2021; Hendi et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Aiken and Holzbaur, 2021 and Hendi et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Cx proteins interact with various actin cytoskeletal regulators including Rap1, IQGAP, ZO-1, Claudin, and Drebrin.
claims.source: Cx proteins have been shown to interact with various actin cytoskeletal regulators including Rap1, IQGAP, ZO-1, Claudin, and Drebrin (Falk et al., 2014; Lasseigne et al., 2021; Olk et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Falk et al., 2014, Lasseigne et al., 2021, and Olk et al., 2009.

claims.claim: RAP-2 small GTPase and its effector kinase MIG-15/TNIK are crucial for the presynaptic tiling of DA8 and DA9 neurons.
claims.source: Indeed, we have previously shown that RAP-2 small GTPase and its effector kinase MIG-15/TNIK is crucial for the presynaptic tiling of the DA8 and DA9 neurons (Chen et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2018.

claims.claim: DD5/DD6 presynaptic tiling defects were not observed in mutants of rap-1/Rap1, rap-2/Rap2, pes-7/IQGAP, zoo-1/ZO-1, vab-9/Claudin, dbn-1/Drebrin, and mig-15/TNIK in the egl-20(n585) background.
claims.source: However, we did not observe DD5/DD6 presynaptic tiling defects in the mutants of rap-1/Rap1, rap-2/Rap2, pes-7/IQGAP, zoo-1/ZO-1, vab-9/Caludin, dbn-1/Drebrin, and mig-15/TNIK in the egl-20(n585) background (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: DD5 and DD6 neurons control presynaptic tiling through an uncharacterized mechanism.
claims.source: Therefore, the DD5 and DD6 neurons seem to control presynaptic tiling through an uncharacterized mechanism.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a conclusion based on the lack of presynaptic tiling defects in known cytoskeletal regulator mutants.

claims.claim: Mutations in gap junction proteins are often associated with various synaptopathies caused by abnormal synapse number and position.
claims.source: Mutations in gap junction proteins are often associated with various synaptopathies caused by abnormal synapse number and position (Lapato and Tiwari-Woodruff, 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lapato and Tiwari-Woodruff, 2018.

claims.claim: The work revealing the novel function of a gap junction protein in presynaptic patterning will help better understand how mutations in gap junction proteins cause synaptopathies.
claims.source: The present work that revealed the novel function of a gap junction protein in presynaptic patterning will help us better understand how mutations in gap junction proteins cause synaptopathies.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a potential impact of the present work.

claims.claim: DD neurons undergo synaptic remodeling at the end of the first larval stage L1, when the dorsal dendrites switch their fates to axons to form presynaptic connections with the dorsal body wall muscles.
claims.source: DD neurons undergo synaptic remodeling at the end of the first larval stage L1, when the dorsal dendrites switch their fates to axons to form presynaptic connections with the dorsal body wall muscles (White et al., 1978).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to White et al., 1978.

claims.claim: At mid L2 stage, egl-20(n585); unc-9(e101) double mutants exhibit presynaptic tiling defects.
claims.source: We showed that at mid L2 stage, egl-20(n585); unc-9(e101) double mutants exhibit presynaptic tiling defects (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: egl-20 and unc-9 are required for the establishment of axonal and presynaptic tiling, respectively.
claims.source: This suggests that egl-20 and unc-9 are required for the establishment of axonal and presynaptic tiling, respectively.
claims.evidence: The claim is stated as a suggestion based on the observation of defects at L2 stage.

claims.claim: The mCherry::RAB-3 puncta at the posterior DD5 axon of egl-20(n585); unc-9(e101) mutants are apposed by NLG-1::AID::GFP.
claims.source: We observed that the mCherry::RAB-3 puncta at the posterior DD5 axon of egl-20(n585); unc-9(e101) mutants are apposed by NLG-1::AID::GFP, similar to those in wild type (Figure 2C and D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Figure 2C and D.

claims.claim: The most posterior portion of the DD5 axon does not contain RAB-3 puncta apposed by NLG-1::AID::GFP in egl-20(n585); unc-9(e101) mutants.
claims.source: The most posterior portion of the DD5 axon did not contain RAB-3 puncta apposed by NLG-1::AID::GFP (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The RAB-3 puncta in the DD5 axon are co-localized with the presynaptic active zone protein UNC-10 in the egl-20(n585); unc-9(e101) double mutant.
claims.source: The RAB-3 puncta in the DD5 axon are co-localized with the presynaptic active zone protein UNC-10 in the egl-20(n585); unc-9(e101) double mutant (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The ectopic RAB-3 puncta formed in the posterior DD5 axon of egl-20(n585); unc-9(e101) double mutant likely represent bona fide synapses.
claims.source: These observations indicate that the ectopic RAB-3 puncta formed in the posterior DD5 axon of egl-20(n585); unc-9(e101) double mutant likely represent bona fide synapses.
